A State of Detransition

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we discover that, for some, the difficulty of gender transitioning didn't end in emotional fulfillment but rather more pain and confusion.

Unique Selling Point:
Detransitioning is, in the words of one of our experts, "under reported". That's probably because it's little researched, an unspoken taboo in some circles and downplayed in others. It might also be because, as some activists claim, it isn't that prevalent. But, the fact is that many experts are warning that not enough attention is being paid to the phenomenon, and that charities are filling the vacuum left by a medical fraternity still grappling with elective gender re-alignment surgery. This story will attempt to shed light on this apparently new and controversial element of an already complex issue.

Summary:
What do you do if, having made the difficult decision to transition from one gender or identity to another, you discover that your're still not happy; that you want to reverse the effects of hormone therapy and - in some instances - surgery? Who do you talk to? How do you begin to deal with the trauma of discovering that the thing you thought would end your misery is making you more depressed?

Gender Dysphoria is far better understood than it was just a few years ago, but it is no less controversial. Not least because many countries are making allowance for what's known as surgery by "affirmation" and making hormone therapy available to ever-younger patients. That said, far less is known about what drives the need to detransition beyond the anecdotal and, in some cases, attempts to better understand it have been met with resistance or contempt. But, the figures quoted in places like the UK suggest more research is needed as a matter of urgency.

In this story we'll meet an outspoken Irish activist who detransitioned several years ago and is dumbstruck by the resistance to attempts to better understand it - not least from the transgender community itself. We'll interview a British Psychotherapist whose attempt to conduct research on the subject was shot down by his University for being un-PC, and we'll speak to a South African transgender psychologist to examine the issue from a local perspective.

3 x train journeys Bristol and London to St Leonard's On-Sea
1 x flight London to Dublin
1 night accommodation for one in London

Script:


VO: I met Amber Barrett in Cape Town in 2015 at around the time she’d decided on gender re-alignment or gender confirmation surgery to transition to female.

Upsound: heading into surgery

VO: I remember thinking how courageous she was, and how surprised I’d been by her almost constant smile. The physical and emotional transformation was remarkable.

Upsound: party, hugs etc

VO: Four years later, she appears content and is in no doubt that transitioning was the right choice. In fact, she wishes she had done it sooner.

Amber Barrett [] STRAP “Amber Barrett”: I feel incredibly happy…

VO: Of course, Amber still encounters challenges but hers is a story about facing down despair; making profound decisions in the pursuit of happiness. But, that’s not how all these stories end.

VO: Some – between one and five percent according to estimates – don’t find happiness during or at the end of their transition and choose to cease or reverse the process. They’re what’s known as detransitioners.

John Skype [00:01:47] So, Debbie, first off, can you give us an idea of why and when you decided to transition?

Debbie [00:01:56] Yeah, it's complicated. Do you know anything about trauma, childhood trauma?

VO: Debbie is a detransitioner. Having transitioned from female to male just under 20 years ago, she’s now trying to reclaim her womanhood. We spoke for 40 minutes, but it was clear that Debbie wanted – perhaps, needed - to talk for longer than that. And yet, the depth of her trauma meant she sometimes struggled for the words that properly described it.

Debbie [00:16:25] …I tried to get work. It's so complicated. I don't even know how to explain.

John Skype [00:17:24] Take your time. It's a complex story, so take your time.

VO: She had sent me a collection of photographs. I recognized in some the features of the person I was talking to now. But it was hard to reconcile the images with the story I was being told. A young girl sexually abused, bullied, manipulated, ignored. Someone at war with herself.

Debbie [00:18:58] STRAP “Debbie” (CUT) I was always, being me was always horrendous. I mean, I actually hated my own body as far back as I can remember. I despised my body. Every bit of my body, I despised it.

VO: It seemed a classic case of what’s known as gender dysphoria…

VO: …a condition where a person experiences distress because there’s a mismatch between their biological sex and gender identity. After more than four decades of unresolved trauma, Debbie found a private psychiatrist in 2002 who confirmed precisely that.

Debbie [00:20:23] (CUT) he said, yeah, yeah, your trans and basically he injected me with testosterone at that first appointment. I was 44 years old.

VO: Testosterone is a male hormone that develops so-called secondary sex characteristics like a deeper voice, a masculine hair pattern, fat and muscle distribution. Once the transition begins, it’s taken continuously. In the 13 years that followed Debbie also had multiple surgeries, including having her breasts, uterus and ovaries removed.

VO: It completed an astonishing transformation. (Pause) The thing is, that’s not where Debbie’s story ends.

John Skype: Did life get better? Did it get easier?

Debbie [00:26:54] I thought in my credulous naivity that in the beginning that if I became a completely different person, all the trauma and (CUT) all the difficulties I've had in life would all just disappear, and I would become this totally confident man. (CUT) But, in reality, that didn't happen.

VO: It didn’t happen says Debbie because she didn’t have gender dysphoria. A different counsellor diagnosed her with complex post-traumatic stress. After a further period of uncertainty, she stopped taking testosterone earlier this year. Her detransition had begun.

VO: It’s an uncertain journey because, right now, establishing the facts around detransitioning, according to some, is being hampered by a climate of intolerance.

LINK (DAY 1): Even the briefest research into detransitioning makes you realise it’s a controversial subject – one that some would prefer to ignore. I’ve come to an English seaside town to speak to someone who knows that better than most.

VO: St Leonard’s-on-Sea is home to psychotherapist, James Caspian. Troubled by what he considered an absence of proper research into detransitioning, he approached a British university in 2016 to try to change that.

James Caspian [00:14:41] I put in a proposal to research people that reversed gender reassignment surgery. It was cleared. I was given permission to go ahead.

VO: After a slow response by potential subjects, he decided to broaden the scope of his research to include people who reverse their gender transition without necessarily reversing their surgery.

VO: This time, his request was turned down. The University was concerned about data protection and privacy - among other things – but also about being attacked on social media because the subject was “politically incorrect”.

John [00:15:57] You've must have fallen over backwards.

James Caspian [00:15:59] I did. I was absolutely shocked that an academic institution could use reasons like that to prevent research.

VO: It pushed the “pause” button on Caspian’s research, but it didn’t stop the conversations.

James Caspian [00:09:31] I've talked to a lot of people who have transitioned who say they think they're very concerned about the transition. (CUT) They're very concerned about stories of young women saying that they felt they were drawn into a kind of a trend and that they personally would counsel anyone considering gender transition to be very cautious and to think very carefully and to really look at themselves and not to think it's going to solve a whole lot of problems that are nothing to do with gender.

VO: The question remains to what extent detransitioning is being driven by an incorrect or rushed gender dysphoria diagnosis, if at all?

James Caspian [00:28:42] there needs to be a body of research over a very long period of time, needs to be peer reviewed and needs to be control groups. It needs to be done in the way that all ethical medical research is done to build up that body of knowledge and at the moment, it isn't there.

VO: The trans community argues detransitioning’s underlying causes include ongoing discrimination and a lack of support during and after transition. Another outspoken psychotherapist says establishing the facts requires more discussion than is happening right now.

Link: (DAY 2) Small town Ireland might not be an obvious place to look into detransitioning, but it’s home to someone with first-hand experience of the subject, and strong views about the debate not being limited to one side.

Stella O’Malley [00:01:24] I think the only way to have the best treatment available for any issue is by discussing. I think talking is the only thing that gets us anywhere in life and I think every civilized society, when they have challenges, need to talk about them.

VO: Like Caspian, Stella O’Malley is worried about the speed with which gender dysphoria is sometimes diagnosed and, in particular, the impact on young people.
Stella O’Malley [00:22:18] STRAP “Psychotherapist & Author” You know, far as back as I can remember, around about three. I thought I was a boy. I thought I should be boy. I thought was a better boy than any boy I knew. And I was very dismissive, funnily enough of so-called tomboys. They don't know what they are doing. I'm the real thing.

VO: This, according to O’Malley, bore all the hallmarks of gender dysphoria. But she’s now a wife and mother; comfortable, she says, in her own skin. Had she been born in the 2000’s, the outcome may have been very different.

Stella O’Malley [00:22:18] I was quite defiant, quite assertive and I think that would have really suited me in this movement and I would have been the kid who said, yeah, I want to be part of this. I am a boy. And I was born in the wrong body. That's my solution, to be a boy.

VO: Referrals to the UK’s only state-run youth gender clinic have risen by 400 percent in the past five years. In some cases they’re prescribed so-called puberty blockers to put the brakes on that phase in their lives until they can make an informed decision as an adult.

Stella O’Malley [00:17:55] this is a heavy route of burden, a burden of medical treatment (CUT). They will have sexual impaired functioning. They may not be able to orgasm and we don't know because there is no research of the impact of not going through biological puberty and instead going through a medical puberty of the opposite sex. We don't know, we are 10 years into this.

VO: Caspian agrees.

James Caspian [00:30:59] CUT we need to completely rethink what we're doing and we need to encourage young people to know that they can experiment with gender and that they can be gender nonconforming and that doesn't necessarily have to mean medical treatment.

VO: And there’s a strong argument for a rethink into the way some adults are treated, too. So vividly and tragically epitomised by Debbie.

Debbie [00:37:55] they've got two boxes M to F, F to M and I'm in the middle and I don't fit. (CUT) I'm stuck. It's horrendous.

ENDS…

But, the figures quoted in places like the UK suggest more research is needed as a matter of urgency. In this story we'll meet an outspoken Irish activist who detransitioned several years ago and is dumbstruck by the resistance to attempts to better understand it - not least from the transgender community itself. We'll interview a British Psychotherapist whose attempt to conduct research on the subject was shot down by his University for being un-PC, and we'll speak to a South African transgender psychologist to examine the issue from a local perspective.
